entries.title: US: Karoline Leavitt to step down as Trump's spokesperson
entries.summary: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is to leave her job at the end of the month, President Donald Trump says. Leavitt, 28, is the youngest-ever person to have held the position.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Karoline Leavitt to step down as Trump's spokesperson

August 13, 2026

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is to leave her job at the end of the month, President Donald Trump says. Leavitt, 28, is the youngest-ever person to have held the position.

Karoline Leavitt, will leave her role as White House press secretary at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said Tuesday.

Leavitt is one of the best-known faces and most ardent defenders of the MAGA movement.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Leavitt was stepping down to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family," adding that it was "a decision I totally understand and respect!"

Who is Karoline Leavitt?

Leavitt, now 28, who took on the job in January 2025 aged 27 at the start of Trump's second term in office, has been the youngest-ever White House press secretary.

She recently returned from parental leave after giving birth to her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a 2-year-old son.

After initially wanting to be a journalist, Leavitt soon entered politics, and joined the White House press office during Trump's first term, working under then-spokeswoman Kayleigh McEnany.

After Trump lost the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, Leavitt worked for the office of Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, a highly-loyal Republican supporter of Trump.

Leavitt later unsuccessfully ran for a seat in the House of Representatives in 2022.

She also worked as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump, before joining his successful 2024 campaign.

'The honor and adventure of a lifetime' — Leavitt

In a post on X, Leavitt waxed lyrical about her period in the job.

"Serving as the White House Press Secretary over the past year and a half has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime," Leavitt wrote.

"I am incredibly grateful to President Trump for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities, such as working in the West Wing and spending countless hours in the Oval Office, flying around the world and meeting foreign leaders, and traveling across our beautiful country and meeting Americans from all walks of life," she added.

She said her "bittersweet decision to depart the White House" was due to the difficulties of combining motherhood with the demands of the White House position.

Leavitt: A devoted defender of Trump

Leavitt, who Trump says will remain "one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," has been a key figure in promoting the president's ideology and views, sometimes stretching the truth to do so.

Her very first press conference, on January 28, 2025, was notable for her false claim that $50 million (€43.4 million) in US taxpayers' money had been earmarked to buy condoms in the Gaza Strip.

Since then, she has staunchly defended Trump's hard-line policies while deflecting questions such as those concerning the president's ties with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She was also known for denigrating mainstream media outlets in line with Trump's hostile attitude to reporters who gainsay him.

Her devotion has brought her consistent praise from the president, who has now called her "one ‌of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Does the clean energy transition need forever chemicals?
entries.summary: As nations globally move to ban forever chemicals, should renewable energy technologies be exempt for the sake of saving the climate?
entries.content:
August 13, 2026

As nations globally move to ban forever chemicals, should renewable energy technologies be exempt for the sake of saving the climate?

From solar panels to wind turbines, batteries and hydrogen cells, many renewable energy technologies driving the energy transition share a common ingredient: a class of man-made substances known as "forever chemicals."

The group contains 10,000 synthetic chemicals also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the environment and can take thousands of years to degrade.

Widely detected in drinking water, exposure to certain levels of PFAS is linked to increased risk of cancer, suppressed immune function, decreased fertility and developmental delays in children.

These health impacts have inspired bans on well-publicized sources of toxic PFAS such as clothing waterproofing sprays, Teflon non-stick cookware, firefighting foam, packaging, and cosmetic products.

While recent bans in France, New Zealand and Denmark target specific PFAS used in consumer products, the European Union wants a broader ban.

The thousands of forever chemicals the EU proposes outlawing includes fluoropolymers, which are valued for their resistance to extreme temperatures, corrosion and UV degradation, and are present in numerous green technologies from lithium-ion batteries to solar panels.

In EV batteries, for example, binders created with PTFE fluoropolymers — also found in Teflon products — are used to coat dry electrodes for greater energy efficiency.

The chemicals industry has pushed back against Europe's mooted ban. An alliance of the world's leading chemical companies, the Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP) says health concerns about "some types of PFAS" are leading to "unwarranted restrictions" on fluoropolymer production and use.

In a statement on its website describing fluoropolymers as "critical in the fight against climate change," the PFP stated that any bans would "hamstring our climate and energy goals by possibly making the transition more expensive or simply impossible."

Are PFAS necessary to fight climate change?

PFP members include the chemicals arm of US multinational conglomerate, 3M — which is being sued more than $2 billion by the Australian government for its firefighting foam that has leached forever chemicals into the environment — and the Chemours Company, which manufacturers Teflon and was established by chemicals powerhouse, Du Pont.

The European Environment Agency (EEA) says these polymers are considered "relatively less problematic" than the building blocks for PFAS known as monomers. This is due to a larger molecular size that "limits their uptake into living cells" and potential toxicity.

Yet fluoropolymers still degrade over time, raising "additional environmental and human health concerns," according to the EEA. Experts say these polymers will inevitably emit PFAS during their life cycle and enter the environment — and living organisms — through weathering and physical stress over long periods.

"I don't think we're going to solve the climate crisis by getting cancer," said Gretchen Salter of US-based Safer States, which lobbies to safeguard the environment from toxic chemicals. "You can't demonstrate that these chemicals aren't going to do harm."

"Since chemical makers cannot escape the fact that these types of PFAS are harming our health, they are trying to claim that they are necessary for the clean energy transition," Salter said, adding that research shows how PFAS themselves fuel climate harm and toxic pollution.

The petrochemical industry accounts for 30% of global industrial energy demand — which is higher than the iron, steel and cement sectors — and generates 18% of the industrial sector's greenhouse gas emissions. Overall, chemicals used to produce everything from pharmaceuticals to fertilisers, plastics, paints, electronics and cleaning products are responsible for around 6% of global emissions.

Salter says PFAS categorized as fluorogases (f-gases) are also being marketed as "climate-friendly" since they are used for clean tech like heat pumps, and in electric car batteries. But PFAS gases, though largely non-flammable, are "now the largest source of PFAS pollution globally," she said.

This is partly due to their global warming impact, which is potentially thousands of times higher than CO2. F-gas leaks can happen throughout a heat pump lifecycle via worn seals and improper maintenance and end-of-life disposal. F-gases are also present in fridges and air-conditioning units as a synthetic coolant, where they can leak too.

Are there PFAS-free green tech alternatives?

According to UK-based Chem Trust, which advocates for safer alternatives to toxic chemicals, a suite of PFAS-free clean energy technology is already on the market, including for heat pumps that are being rolled out across Europe as part of a transition from gas heating.

Instead of relying on f-gases, propane is just one alternative energy efficient refrigerant for domestic heat pumps, and with the right design has a negligible fire risk, notes a 2025 Chem Trust report.

The group also says several companies are now producing solar cells without fluoropolymers. Equally, polymer paint that protects wind turbine blades and makes them more efficient is available PFAS-free.

"We are seeing more companies in the EU and across the world embrace the challenge of developing PFAS-free green technologies," said Shubhi Sharma, scientific researcher at Chem Trust, in a statement.

But a Europe plastics and chemical lobby group, Plastics Europe, released an assessment report of PFAS-free substitutes in May that argued that "in many critical uses" such as transport, electronics and semiconductors, these alternatives are "either not available or simply do not match the necessary criteria to be considered a viable alternative to fluoropolymers."

Gretchen Salter of Safer States says efforts to exempt so-called critical and low concern PFAS from class-wide bans means "destroying any sort of incentive to switch to safer alternatives."

"As long as the chemicals industry insists that there are no alternatives, there will be no market to develop any," said the campaigner.

Chemours insists that its fluoropolymers and f-gases are "made and used with minimal environmental impact," and says it will achieve a 99% PFAS emissions reduction in the manufacture of fluorinated organic compounds by the end of the decade compared to 2018.

Liz Hitchcock, director of the federal policy program at US environment nonprofit, Toxic-Free Future, told DW that the extreme persistence of PFAS in the environment will inevitably lead to human exposure.

"We've heard claims that there are better PFAS, there are safer PFAS, but we haven't seen the proof."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Russia's Putin angers Japan with 1st visit to Kuril Islands
entries.summary: Japan says it "strongly protests" Russian President Vladimir Putin's trip to the disputed Kuril Islands. Tensions over the Russian-controlled archipelago, claimed partly by Japan, have long dogged bilateral ties.
entries.content:
Asia

Russia's Putin angers Japan with 1st visit to Kuril Islands

August 13, 2026

Japan says it "strongly protests" Russian President Vladimir Putin's trip to the disputed Kuril Islands. Tensions over the Russian-controlled archipelago, claimed partly by Japan, have long dogged bilateral ties.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the far-eastern Kuril Islands for the first time, state media reported on Thursday, drawing anger from Japan.

Japan has long claimed ownership of four of the Kuril Islands, including the one reportedly visited by Putin, which the Soviet Union seized toward the end of World War II.  

What is the dispute over the Kuril Islands?

During his trip, Putin visited a fish-processing plant on the island, known as Iturup in Russian and Etorofu in Japanese, where he was given caviar, Russian media reported.

The island belongs to four that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories and that are now Russian-occupied following the Soviet Union's takeover in 1945.

At that time, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people, with the islands now inhabited by some 20,000 Russian citizens.

The unresolved dispute was one of the key reasons why Moscow and Tokyo never signed a formal World War II peace treaty.

Russian-Japanese relations have since suffered another major blow following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022.

The volcanic Kuril archipelago runs in an arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island of Hokkaido.

What has Japan said about Putin's visit?

In a statement on Thursday, Japan's foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, expressed Tokyo's great displeasure at Putin's visit.

"The Northern Territories ... are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," the statement said.

Strategically-located Kuril Islands

The islands have seldom been visited by Russian leaders, with then-President Dmitry Medvedev in 2010 becoming the first to travel to the disputed territory.

Medvedev also went there in 2015 as prime minister.

Putin's visit to the Kurils came after he visited the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.

The islands had considerable strategic importance for the Soviet Union, which kept a large military presence there during the Cold War amid tensions with the US and Japan.

Talks on the territorial issue that have been held since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 have so far borne no fruit.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: How North Korea has profited from its support for Russia
entries.summary: Exceptionally high revenues, particularly from war aid for Russia, are consolidating the power of North Korea's autocratic leader. A small number of people in the country are benefiting from an economic boom.
entries.content:
North Korea

How North Korea has profited from its support for Russia

August 13, 2026

Exceptionally high revenues, particularly from war aid for Russia, are consolidating the power of North Korea's autocratic leader. A small number of people in the country are benefiting from an economic boom.

For years, satellite images of North Korea at night showed only a few small patches of light. Electricity shortages meant that even cities remained dark. In the six years since April 2020, however, the illuminated area in the center of Pyongyang has tripled in size.

The information portal NK News sees the increased illumination of the urban area as evidence that the regime has prioritized the supply of electricity to new streets and houses in the center to showcase its achievements.

At the last party congress in 2021, Kim Jong Un, North Korea's leader, announced that he would build 50,000 new apartments in the capital. And he did embark on the plan: in the new neighborhood of Hwasong, for example, with the construction of two 40-story apartment blocks shaped like Hwasong intercontinental ballistic missiles.

The new high-rise districts are not the only sign of North Korea's improved prosperity. People who have been visiting Pyongyang for a long time report that the city now appears more modern.

There are many imported cars, including electric cars from China, smartphone apps with QR codes to make payments or to call taxis, and department stores that stock Western fashion brands and cosmetics.

The regime has completed construction in Pyongyang of the biggest hospital in the country and a hothouse the size of New York's Central Park. In June 2025, Kim officially opened the five-kilometer-long (3.3 miles) beach resort of Wonsan-Kalma on the east coast, with space for 20,000 guests.

In June, the Wall Street Journal described North Korea as the "world's most unlikely growth story."

North Korea's lucrative war deals with Russia

The dictatorship is presumably able to finance this sudden upturn thanks to the substantial income from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine.

According to a report by the South Korean Institute for National Security Strategy (INSS) in March, North Korea earns between $7.7 billion and $14.4 billion (€6.7 billion and €12.5 billion) from the sale of munitions to Moscow and the deployment of troops. Bloomberg Economics recently estimated that between 2022 and 2025, North Korea earned more than $14 billion by providing military support for Russia.

Furthermore, it brought in another $8 billion through trade with China, the provision of North Korean workers to other countries, export business and online criminality. The hacking of the ByBit platform in February 2025 was one of the world's biggest cryptocurrency heists. Suspected North Korean hackers made off with $1.5 billion worth of Ethereum, a network with its own virtual currency. In comparison: the previous year, North Korea's entire GDP was $27 billion.

North Korea's involvement in Russia's war effort

It is unclear whether it was Russia or North Korea who first had the idea of using the impoverished country's massive stockpiles of munitions in Russia's war against Ukraine.

Kyiv estimates that in 2024 and 2025, North Korea supplied half the munitions Russia used at the front, as well as self-propelled guns, multiple rocket launchers and ballistic missiles. Ukraine says North Korea is currently planning to transfer a missile unit to Russia to fight against Ukraine, consisting of 90 soldiers, six launch pads and up to 120 missiles.

Between 16,000 and 22,000 North Korean soldiers are already helping Russia to drive Ukraine out of the border province of Kursk and clear the area of mines afterward. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Kim now intends to station a further 30,000 to 50,000 soldiers in Russia.

The business is a lucrative one: The INSS report says that, every month, Kim receives $2,800 per North Korean soldier, $3,000 for an officer and $6,000 to $10,000 for every soldier killed in action.

As in Soviet times, the reciprocal arrangement is conducted primarily through exchange transactions. In exchange for munitions, arms and soldiers, Russia supplies North Korea with crude oil and oil products, grain and military goods from anti-aircraft systems to the technologies for building drones, missiles and submarines.

North Korea's new global stage

Kim's new role as Russia's supporter has given him greater political importance and military power, as demonstrated by the launch of two 5,000-ton destroyers. In all 15 of the years he has been in power, the autocratic leader has never had this much influence, or this much money.

It's an astonishing turnaround. Kim noticeably lost weight during the COVID-19 pandemic, and at the Workers' Party congress in 202,1 he shed tears as he admitted that the national economic development strategy had fallen "far short in almost all sectors."

At the next party congress five years later, with seven rows of artillery pieces lined up outside the building, Kim crowed, "Everything has fundamentally changed."

The partnership with Russia has allowed North Korea to shed its status as a pariah of world politics and overcome its isolation. In June 2024, the Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Kim in Pyongyang. Chinese leader Xi Jinping came in June of this year, three months after the Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko. In September 2025, Kim was in attendance at the celebrations in Beijing, alongside Xi and Putin, to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II.

Profits not reaching North Koreans

However, observers say this economic upswing is not benefiting the majority of the population.

Many households already in a precarious situation and without access to foreign currency have been hit hard by rising food prices and the devaluation of the won, the national currency. In many families, the women, too, must now go out to work in order to maintain living standards.

In the spring of 2024, Kim promoted a "20x10" development program for regions beyond the well-supplied capital Pyongyang. Presumably, he intends to finance this with the new additional revenue. The plan foresees that modern factories will be built in 20 cities or regions annually, creating 200 regional industrial projects over 10 years.

But according to Andrei Lankov, a professor and North Korea expert at Kookmin University in Seoul, the majority of the 20x10 projects fail.

"This is because not only do the factories have no infrastructure, they also do not take into account the mechanisms for supplying electricity, equipment, and raw materials," he said.

The factories are operated according to the principles of a planned economy, which is unsuited to small and medium-sized businesses.

"Unlike the economic growth that took place in North Korea in the mid-2010s, the current growth was based not on internal economic reforms, but only on international good fortune," Lankov said.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Brazil orders Discord to halt livestreaming after teen death
entries.summary: Brazil has ordered Discord to suspend livestreaming as authorities scrutinize how the platform protects young users. The move follows a case described a "real-life horror show" that has triggered national outrage.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

Brazil has ordered Discord to suspend livestreaming as authorities scrutinize how the platform protects young users. The move follows a case described a "real-life horror show" that has triggered national outrage.

Brazil's data protection authority on Wednesday ordered the online messaging platform Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature in the country within three business days.

Officials cited failures to protect children and teenagers from content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide.

Why has Brazil ordered Discord to suspend livestreaming?

The National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) issued the measure after the death of a 13-year-old girl who investigators say was encouraged to harm herself and take her own life during a livestream on the platform.

"Live streams have been repeatedly used to facilitate violence, harassment, and the incitement of self-harm and suicide," said the ANPD.

It cited "robust evidence that the company failed to adopt reasonable measures" to protect children and teenagers from such content.

The regulator said Discord's "Go Live" feature would remain suspended until the company could demonstrate that effective technical, security and governance safeguards for minors were in place.

The ANPD said Discord lacked real-time access to livestream content, limiting its ability to automatically detect violations and leaving it reliant on user reports and other systems the regulator considers inadequate.

Discord has 10 business days to appeal the decision. It could face fines of up to 50 million reais ($9.7 million, €8.4 million) per violation if irregularities are confirmed.

What happened to the 13-year-old girl on Discord?

Police said the 13-year-old girl was encouraged during a roughly 45-minute livestream in July to harm herself and then die by suicide.

Authorities say members of an online group first encouraged her to carry out escalating violent "challenges," including harming an animal, before challenging her to broadcast her own suicide on Discord.

Police say the group deliberately sought out emotionally vulnerable children and teenagers.

Five teenagers and one adult were detained in connection with the case. Police said another girl who was allegedly preparing to take her own life during a livestream was also rescued during the investigation.

What has been the wider reaction in Brazil?

Brazil's Justice Ministry and police have criticized Discord's moderation and age-control systems. One official said one person involved in the case had been able to register an age of 148 using the platform's self-declaration system.

Brazilian first lady Rosangela "Janja" da Silva last week called for Discord to be completely blocked in the country following the teenager's death.

Discord representatives met Brazilian authorities on Friday and later submitted a plan aimed at strengthening protections for users under 18.

Brazil has tightened rules governing children's use of online platforms, including requirements on age verification and parental links for younger users.

*Editor's note: If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://www.befrienders.org/

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
entries.summary: A Eurovision victory will no longer guarantee hosting rights if war or a wider security crisis affects the winning country. The change could have particular significance for recent high-flyers Ukraine and Israel.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

A Eurovision victory will no longer guarantee hosting rights if war or a wider security crisis affects the winning country. The change could have particular significance for recent high-flyers Ukraine and Israel.

Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event.

Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition.

What did the Eurovision organizers say?

Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).

Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said.

The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected.

Why is the Eurovision changing the rules?

The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026.

Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza. Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran.

The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before.

Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.

Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

What else is changing about the Eurovision?

Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists.

Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices.

The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live.

Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent.

Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Russia: Why is the Yabloko party barred from the elections?
entries.summary: Russia's supreme court has banned the anti-war opposition party Yabloko from September's parliamentary elections. What does this mean for the election campaign, opponents of the war and for the political mood in Russia?
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Why is the Yabloko party barred from the elections?

August 12, 2026

Russia's supreme court has banned the anti-war opposition party Yabloko from September's parliamentary elections. What does this mean for the election campaign, opponents of the war and for the political mood in Russia?

On Monday Russia's supreme court upheld a lawsuit against the anti-war opposition party Yabloko. Its candidates will now be barred from taking part in the parliamentary elections on September 18 to 20.

The case against Yabloko was brought by the pro-Kremlin party Rodina, which accused it of infringing copyright with its election campaign materials. Rodina also made the claim that Yabloko had engaged in extremist activities and had received illegal financing from abroad.

The verdict was pronounced by presiding judge Vyacheslav Kirillov. This was the same judge who, in April, banned the Russian human rights organization Memorial and designated it an extremist organization. Kirillov also previously dismissed legal complaints against the Russian prison service filed by the prominent opposition politician Alexei Navalny. Navalny spent many years in Russian prisons prior to his death in jail in 2024.

At least 500 people gathered in front of the Supreme Court to show their support for Yabloko. They distributed apples and sang songs. The name Yabloko – "apple" in English – derives from the initials of the party's three founders, Grigory Yavlinsky, Yury Boldyrev and Vladimir Lukin (YaBL). The apple is now well-known as a symbol of the party.

At the end of the nine-hour court session, security services threatened the people gathered outside the courthouse with arrest, also warning young men that they could be taken to an army enlistment office.

"You are mistaken if you believe that, with a stroke of a pen, you can write off millions of people who want peace, freedom and a normal future for their country," Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Yabloko, wrote on Telegram that evening.

He insisted that the party had not broken any Russian laws, and announced that he would appeal the judgement.

The Kremlin 'got scared'

Grigory Yavlinsky, one of the founders of Yabloko, said those in power were afraid of Yabloko's program, which calls for an election "for peace, freedom and a life without fear" – because, he said, "removing a party with a platform like this from the election, without any real grounds, is the political system exposing itself."

The lawsuit came at the same time as an appeal by Russian opposition and cultural leaders living abroad for people to support Yabloko.

They include the politician Yulia Navalnaya, Alexei Navalny's widow, as well as Lyubov Sobol, Ilya Yashin and Andrei Pivovarov. The writer Dmitry Bykov, human rights activist Oleg Orlov and other prominent people also voiced their support for Yabloko.

Navalnaya, who now leads the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) her husband set up in 2011, responded to the verdict. The Kremlin was originally going to let Yabloko stand in the elections, she said, but those in power "got scared" and had the party blocked.

Navalnaya wrote on Telegram that the powers-that-be had observed a development they wanted to stop at any cost: People were starting to join forces. This, she wrote, was less about support for Yabloko than the possibility for millions of Russians to express how they really felt about Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine.

Andrei Pivovarov, a political activist who lives in exile in Germany and is a coordinator of the Russian Antiwar Committee, explained to DW that the opposition had not believed supporting Yabloko would bring about swift political change or an end to the war. The aim, he said, had been to make visible the extent of anti-war sentiment in Russia.

"There would have been a dozen parties on the ballot who are pro-war, and one that is pro-peace. The war wouldn't end even if Yabloko were to get representatives into the State Duma. But we would have seen that a lot of Russians oppose the war," said Pivovarov. This view, he added, would not simply disappear now Yabloko has been barred from standing.

What were the Kremlin's plans for Yabloko?

The political scientist Ivan Preobrazhensky speculated in an interview with DW that the banning of Yabloko could be a consequence of a power struggle between different interest groups in the Kremlin. He suggested that the security bloc allied with the federal security service, the FSB, may have wanted Yabloko to act as a counterweight to the New People party. This is regarded as a project of Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of the presidential administration.

Another version of events is that Kiriyenko himself may have tried to create the impression of political rivalry, and underestimated the potential of anti-war feeling in the country.

Preobazhensky says the government underestimated the number of people in Russia who oppose the war and are ready to support a political force campaigning for an end to the war in Ukraine. Surveys, he says, indicate that there is substantial demand for such a political alternative. He also believes that the Kremlin initially intended to let Yabloko run in the election but changed its mind when it saw how much support the party was getting.

Another political scientist, Mikhail Vinogradov, thinks there was a different calculation behind the move. If Yabloko had scored very few votes in the election, the Kremlin could have painted a picture of a population solidly behind the war. A poor result would also have served to disillusion those who oppose it.

Barring Yabloko makes independent election monitoring more difficult. The party is now no longer allowed to send representatives to monitor polling stations. Roman Udot, a Russian specialist in electoral observation, explains that Yabloko has also enabled access for independent observers in the past.

Does the Kremlin have the situation under control?

The State Duma elections are taking place at a time of growing uncertainty in Russian society, says Margarita Zavadskaya from the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. She points to data from the Russian Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), which regularly records the population's prevailing view of the situation in the country: optimism or alarm?

At the end of July, 57% of those surveyed said that they were worried. This is the highest level since mobilization in the autumn of 2022. FOM surveys should be taken with a grain of salt, but Zavadskaya says an increase like this in high summer indicates that "something is not going according to plan."

She gives the increase in drone attacks, deaths, fires in warehouses and rumors of a fresh mobilization as the reasons, and comments that the summer of 2026 has been the most unsettling for the people in Russia since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. She also believes the number of people who support the war is going down rather than up.

The Russian leadership therefore has good reason to be nervous.

"For the Kremlin, the ideal scenario would be a boring election with low turnout and no noteworthy events," says Zavadskaya. "Right now, though, this seems unlikely, as the situation in the run-up to the election does not appear normal, nor does it give the impression that the government has the situation under control."

This article was originally written in Russian.

entries.title: 25 years Ohrid Agreement: Is N. Macedonia's peace holding?
entries.summary: A quarter of a century after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended North Macedonia's 2001 conflict, analysts warn that peace between ethnic communities remains fragile.
entries.content:
North Macedonia

25 years Ohrid Agreement: Is N. Macedonia's peace holding?

August 12, 2026

A quarter of a century after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended North Macedonia's 2001 conflict, analysts warn that peace between ethnic communities remains fragile.

The guns fell silent in 2001, but North Macedonia is still grappling with the legacy of its ethnic conflict.

Twenty-five years after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended the fighting, ethnic Macedonians and Albanians live in peace, yet analysts say genuine reconciliation remains unattained.

The six-month conflict that erupted in February 2001 is often described as the final chapter of former Yugoslavia's violent breakup.

But unlike the wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it was contained before it could spiral into a larger tragedy, thanks in large part to a political compromise brokered by NATO, the United States and leading EU countries.

Agreement enters a new phase

Тwenty-five years later, the political order that emerged from the Ohrid Framework Agreement is entering a new phase.

When the conservative Macedonian VMRO-DPMNE party returned to power two years ago, the Democratic Union for Integration (DUI), the main ethnic Albanian party, went into opposition.

This development ended two decades of governing influence for Ali Ahmeti, who transformed himself from leader of the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army (NLA) during the 2001 conflict into one of the country's most influential political figures.

Ahmeti, who swapped his guerrilla uniform for tailored black suits and white shirts after the Ohrid Agreement, now argues that ethnic relations have deteriorated over the past two years.

"Attacks on the official use of the Albanian language, the abolition of equitable and adequate representation, the weakening of mechanisms designed to prevent majoritarian rule and the promotion of a monoethnic concept of the state are serious signals about the direction in which the country is moving," he said in a statement marking August 2, North Macedonia's national holiday.

Balancing ethnic diversity and political stability

Home to a large ethnic Albanian minority, North Macedonia has spent much of the past quarter-century trying to balance its ethnic diversity within a stable political system.

According to the latest census, Albanians make up over a quarter of North Macedonia's population of 1.8 million.

For Bujar Osmani, a senior DUI official and former foreign minister, the key question is no longer how much of the Ohrid Agreement has been implemented, but whether its gains can be preserved.

"On the 25th anniversary of the Ohrid Agreement, the question is no longer only what we have implemented since 2001. The question is whether we will allow, within a few years, the dismantling of what has kept North Macedonia stable for two and a half decades," he told DW.

2001: A wound that has not fully healed

The legacy of the 2001 conflict runs deep.

The fighting claimed the lives of 72 soldiers and police officers, while the number of ethnic Albanian insurgents killed remains disputed, with estimates ranging from about 100 to several hundred. More than 170,000 people were displaced, including 74,000 within the country.

The Ohrid Framework Agreement that ended the conflict reshaped North Macedonia's political system, introducing power-sharing mechanisms designed to give minority communities a greater voice in decision-making.

Laws affecting sensitive issues such as language, education and national symbols require support not only from a parliamentary majority but also from representatives of minority groups.

While largely in line with European standards on minority rights, the arrangement did not end disputes over equality and representation.

"The agreement achieved a large part of its historic mission, but its essence cannot be declared complete," Osmani said. "Ohrid is not an administrative checklist that can be fulfilled once and then archived. It is a system of balance that must be respected continuously."

Macedonian majority also voices grievances

At the heart of the debate are differing views on Ohrid's legacy.

While many ethnic Macedonians argue that affirmative representation policies have created unfair advantages for Albanians, Albanian politicians say the real concern is the gradual erosion of rights secured under the agreement.

"There is discrimination that frustrates many in the Macedonian community because Albanians are often given priority in recruitment to meet representation quotas in the public sector," said Stojance Angelov, a police general during the 2001 conflict.

Angelov said such practices put ethnic affiliation ahead of qualifications.

Osmani rejects that narrative, arguing that recent government policies have weakened protections for Albanians that were introduced after the conflict.

"At first, all of this was concealed behind political propaganda, technical explanations and claims that it was merely modernization of the system. Today, as that noise gradually fades, it is becoming much clearer what is actually being called into question," he said.

Defensive nationalism on the rise

Domestic and international observers warn that years of political crises and disputes over national identity have slowed reforms and reinforced ethnic divisions.

Harald Schenker of the German peacebuilding organization Pro Peace says the Ohrid Agreement transformed North Macedonia's institutions, but not necessarily relations between its communities.

"Ethnic distance is increasing, the education system remains segregated, and the two communities understand each other less and less," he told DW.

According to Schenker, the agreement created new institutions and rules of governance but failed to foster reconciliation or a shared vision for the future.

"Each side maintains its own interpretation of what happened in 2001," he said. "Twenty-five years on, there is a need for platforms where people can discuss these differences openly. Different perspectives exist, but people need to talk to one another."

Stalled EU integration

At the same time, years of stalled EU integration have fueled uncertainty about the country's direction. Although North Macedonia became an EU candidate country in 2005, negotiations have still not formally begun.

After overcoming a decades-long dispute with Greece over its name, North Macedonia has faced new obstacles stemming from Bulgaria's demands relating to history, language and national identity.

The prolonged stalemate has not only frustrated reform efforts but has also deepened interethnic tensions, as the fading prospect of EU membership has removed one of the few unifying projects shared by both Macedonians and Albanians.

Against that backdrop, questions about North Macedonia's future remain closely tied to the legacy of the Ohrid Agreement. Next month, the country will mark 35 years since independence from the former Yugoslavia.

Osmani does not believe the country faces the risk of a new conflict but warns that ethnic tensions can build gradually.

"I do not believe citizens want a new problem," he said. "But ethnic tensions do not begin with conflict. They begin when one community gradually loses confidence that the system treats it as an equal."

Angelov shares that view.

"For me, the greatest achievement is that, whereas we once looked at each other through rifle sights, today I drink coffee with some of the veteran fighters of the Albanian NLA," he said.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: No oil, no salary: Iraqi state employees are feeling the crunch of the Hormuz blockade
entries.summary: Because of the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq cannot export enough oil to fund the country's huge public sector. Protests have already started. Will the Iran war destabilize Iraq again?
entries.content:
Iraq

Due to the Iran war, Iraq is running out of money

August 12, 2026

Because of the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq cannot export enough oil to fund the country's huge public sector. Protests have already started. Will the Iran war destabilize Iraq again?

They may be thousands of kilometers away but the Strait of Hormuz — or more specifically, its blockade — is making life increasingly difficult for many ordinary Iraqis.

For the last three months or so, Mahmoud Waleed's salary has been arriving later and later. The 38-year-old teacher is paid by the Iraqi Ministry of Education, but because Iraq cannot export enough oil through the Strait of Hormuz, the government is running out of cash.

As a result, thousands of Iraqis like Waleed are not being paid on time.

"The delay affects you a lot," the Mosul local told DW. "Like most people, we have financial obligations as well as basic living expenses. We're just more and more convinced that we need to reduce expenses and keep some money aside for emergencies — just until things return to normal. It makes you really anxious and fearful."

"The future looks more uncertain," adds Ahmed, a doctor from the same city who didn't want to give DW his full name for personal reasons. "This month, our salaries were delayed by more than 10 days. The Minister of Health explained the state doesn't have sufficient cash flow and that's why there was a delay. But we just don't know how long the next delay will be."

In early August, there were a number of small demonstrations about the delayed salaries. Staff from universities around the country protested as did employees at the Ministry of Electricity.

Why doesn't Iraq have cash for salaries?

Almost all of Iraq's national budget, somewhere between 85% and 90%, comes from the export of its oil.

At the same time, Iraq has a huge and growing public sector, with about two-thirds of the around 30 million working-age Iraqis relying on the state for their livelihoods. That's why the majority of the state budget now goes towards salaries, pensions and social welfare; every month the Iraqi government needs somewhere between $6.5 billion and $8.2 billion for those payments.

But recently that money has become much harder to find.

Since Israel and the US bombed Iran in late February, Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Almost all of Iraq's oil — between 80% to 90% — was shipped out through there because unlike other countries in the region, Iraq doesn't have significant alternative routes.

As a result of the blockade, Iraqi oil exports decreased by around 83% in March, compared to the same period last year. By May, Iraq's seaborne crude exports were down 97%.

This means Iraq's national income has also been severely reduced. Government sources told various local media that Iraq's monthly income in May and June was somewhere between $2 billion and $2.3 billion, far less than is needed.

It's that kind of news that recently led to panicked rumors that state salaries would only be paid every 45 days, instead of each month.

Over the past few days, the Iraqi government put out several statements, firstly denying the 45-day rumor and then saying it still had $83 billion in reserves, plus gold holdings and non-oil income. This means salaries can be paid for the next 10 to 11 months, it said on Tuesday.

However that might not be enough. A report by UK advisory firm Oxford Economics this week noted that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is unlikely to return to normal anytime soon.

"Until at least 2028, traffic levels are expected to fluctuate as tensions ebb and flow, while on average remaining well below pre-conflict norms," Ben May, director of global macro research said in a statement.

This is a serious crisis, one which "transcends the oil sector," Iraqi economist Ali Al-Rawi argued in an August report for Baghdad-based think tank the Al Bayan Center. "The entirety of the Iraqi economy is now hostage to… oil revenues."

Iraq destabilized?

None of the state employees DW spoke to were planning to attend protests if their salaries were delayed again.

And right now, this situation is unlikely to destabilize Iraq, Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW.

"If salary delays continue, I would expect more protests, but initially they are likely to remain sectoral rather than develop into another nationwide movement like Tishreen," al-Shakeri said, referring to huge youth-led, anti-government protests between 2019 and 2021. "The government has learned from 2019 and now has a range of political, administrative and security mechanisms to contain protests before they broaden."

Things could get more dangerous later though if a combination of different problems arise, some of which have sparked larger protests in the past.

"If salary delays are combined with electricity shortages, inflation and deteriorating services over a sustained period, these separate protests could begin to connect," al-Shakeri predicts. "At that point, Iraq's recent stability would face a much more serious test."

What can Iraq do?

Iraq has tried to work around its Strait of Hormuz problem. A small proportion of Iraqi oil is exported via a Turkish pipeline. Oil has also been trucked out of Iraq, then loaded onto ships at Syrian ports. Last week, the Iraqi government announced it was reviving a long-shuttered Iraq-Lebanon pipeline.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi also said that when he visited Iran in late July, he asked Iranian officials for special dispensation allowing Iraqi oil to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The two countries have a good relationship. 

Far more important, experts say, is that the new Iraqi government finally implement realistic reforms, measures that reduce corruption and encourage the private sector, moving the country away from oil dependency and offering locals jobs outside of the civil service.

But reforms also require funding — and the latest statistics indicate that this is not what is happening, researchers at economic consultancy Iraqi Horizons wrote this month.

In May, total government expenditure fell by around a quarter compared to last year. Of that, money for salaries, pensions and social security accounted for 99% of all operational spending. Which means there's very little cash left for anything else, the consultants pointed out.

"Fiscal crises have pushed Iraqi governments towards reform before," al-Shakeri from Chatham House suggested. "When oil revenues fall, governments become more willing to discuss combatting corruption, increasing non-oil revenues and supporting the private sector. But once oil money begins flowing again, the political incentives for reform weaken."

The current crisis could create an opening for reform in Iraq, al-Shakeri concluded. "But whether those openings survive once the immediate pressure eases is the real question."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Mozart tribute ends on sour note after mass figurine theft
entries.summary: A playful tribute to Mozart has turned into a whodunit after 210 gold-colored figures disappeared from one of Austria's busiest tourist spots. The mass theft forced organizers to end the outdoor display early.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

A playful tribute to Mozart has turned into a whodunit after 210 gold-colored figures disappeared from one of Austria's busiest tourist spots. The mass theft forced organizers to end the outdoor display early.

More than 200 gold-colored Mozart figures have vanished from a public art installation in Salzburg, forcing organizers to end part of the exhibition early.

The theft has disrupted a major public art project marking the 270th anniversary of composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's birth in his home city.

What do we know about the theft of the mini-Mozarts?

The Mozarteum Foundation said 210 of the 320 figures installed in the city's Mirabell Garden had disappeared. The theft forced organizers to end the garden display early.

Organizers had kept some replacements in reserve, but not enough to offset the scale of the theft.

The manufacturer is also on summer holiday, leaving no quick way to replace them.

Several dozen figures remain on display at the Mozarteum and Mozart's birthplace until the end of August.

The figures had been placed in the Mirabell Garden and at several Mozart-related sites around Austria's fourth-largest city.

The polymer figures show Mozart with his dog Pimperl, a nod to the composer's everyday life in Salzburg.

German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl, who is behind the display, said he wanted to show Mozart not as a monument but "as a normal human being despite his genius."

Who might have taken the mini-Mozarts?

Hörl is known for installations made up of large numbers of identical figures depicting famous personalities.

"The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves," Hörl said.

Hörl said he did not believe tourists had simply walked off with the 50-centimeter (20-inch) figures.

"This is organized theft," he said, suggesting they were probably taken at night after the garden had closed. "I find it a bit cheeky."

Hörl had planned to sell the figures after the exhibition for around €90 each, putting the loss at roughly €20,000.

A previous Hörl display in Bayreuth suffered a similar fate when 100 figures of composer Richard Wagner disappeared.

"That's just the nature of public space," Hörl said. "When you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn't complain about what is happening there. It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse
